title: 三十多岁才学开车
title_en: Bad at Being a Beginner: Learning to Drive in My Thirties
summary_zh: 作者三十多岁才学车，发现真正难的不是技术，而是在别人面前当一个“新手”。这篇随笔谈成年人重新学习时的自尊心，也教你用英语写有层次的自我反思。
body: Learning to drive in your thirties is an education in humility that nobody warns you about. Teenagers, whatever their nerves, tend to approach the wheel with a cheerful sense that the world will get out of their way. Adults bring something heavier into the car: years of watching other people drive, a fairly detailed knowledge of what can go wrong, and a reputation for competence that they would rather not lose in front of a stranger. My instructor, a patient woman who hummed quietly whenever I stalled, noticed this within minutes. After our second lesson she told me, kindly but firmly, that I was not bad at driving so much as bad at being a beginner. Whereas at work I was used to knowing the answers, in the car I was paying someone to watch me mix up left and right at a roundabout. Treating each mistake as information rather than as a verdict on my character made the lessons almost enjoyable. I began keeping a small notebook in the glove box, recording one thing I had done badly and one thing I had done well after every drive. Unless you have been an adult beginner at something, it is hard to explain how much that second column mattered. There were setbacks, of course. I failed my first test for drifting too close to a parked van, and spent the evening composing a dignified explanation for friends who had not asked for one. Yet the second attempt felt different, not because my driving had improved dramatically, but because I had stopped needing to look competent. The real lesson, I suspect, extends well beyond the car. Most of us arrange our adult lives so that we rarely have to be visibly bad at anything. Choosing to learn something new in public, at an age when you are supposed to have things figured out, is uncomfortable precisely because it strips that protection away. It is also, I am now convinced, one of the more useful things a grown-up can do.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what made learning to drive hard as an adult?
options: Adults react more slowly than teenagers do
It was difficult to accept being visibly bad at something
The instructor was too impatient with every mistake
There was not enough time to practise between lessons
questions.evidence: I was not bad at driving so much as bad at being a beginner

questions.prompt: What does "that second column" refer to?
options: The list of mistakes made on each drive
The notes the instructor wrote after every lesson
The record of what had gone well after each drive
The explanation written for friends after the failed test
questions.evidence: recording one thing I had done badly and one thing I had done well after every drive

vocabulary.example: Living abroad taught me a certain humility about my own habits.
Her calm competence made everyone in the team feel safer.

vocabulary.meaning: 裁决；（对某人某事的）定论
vocabulary.example: The final verdict on the new café was positive.
Every big project comes with a few setbacks.
He gave a dignified reply to a very rude question.

expressions.note: 字面是“让开”，这里引申为年轻人觉得世界会为他们让路，带点调侃。

expressions.text: not bad at driving so much as bad at being a beginner
expressions.meaning: 与其说不会开车，不如说不会当新手
expressions.note: not A so much as B：纠正对问题本质的误判，书面和口语都很地道。
mix up A and B 指把两样东西搞混：I always mix up their names.

expressions.text: rather than as a verdict on my character
expressions.meaning: 而不是把它看作对我人品的定论
expressions.note: treat A as X rather than as Y：重新看待一件事的常用句式。

expressions.meaning: 把人生（事情）都想明白、安排好了
expressions.note: 口语常说 I don't have it all figured out，带点自嘲。
strip sth away 表示“剥去、去除”，常用于抽象的伪装、保护、自尊。

knowledge.quote: Treating each mistake as information rather than as a verdict on my character made the lessons almost enjoyable.
knowledge.explanation: 整个动名词短语 Treating ... character 作主语，谓语 made 用单数。用动名词开头，可以把一种“做法”当作讨论对象；结尾的 Choosing to learn ... is uncomfortable 也是同样结构。

knowledge.quote: Whereas at work I was used to knowing the answers, in the car I was paying someone to watch me mix up left and right at a roundabout.
knowledge.explanation: whereas 引导对比状语从句，把两个场景并排放：工作中的“胸有成竹”和车里的“手忙脚乱”。比 but 更正式，强调两者截然相反。

knowledge.quote: Unless you have been an adult beginner at something, it is hard to explain how much that second column mattered.
knowledge.explanation: unless = if ... not：“除非你当过成年新手，否则很难体会”。unless 从句里用现在完成时 have been，表示到目前为止的经历。

speaking: 用 1 分钟讲一件你成年后才开始学的事（乐器、运动、语言），说说最难的是技术还是心态，用上 not A so much as B 和 Unless you have ...。
writing: 写一篇 200–250 词的随笔，谈“做新手”的感受，至少用一个动名词主语（如 Admitting ... is ...）、一个 whereas 对比句和一个 unless 条件句。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 Whereas at ... I was used to ..., at/in ... I was ... 对比你在两个不同场合的状态。
task.model: Whereas at work I was used to knowing the answers, in the car I was paying someone to watch me mix up left and right at a roundabout.

title: 一个好的道歉由什么组成
title_en: The Anatomy of an Apology That Actually Works
summary_zh: 说“对不起”很容易，道歉道得好却很难。这篇解说文拆解三种常见的失败道歉，并总结有效道歉的几个要素和时机。读完你能更得体地用英语认错、修复关系。
body: Most of us learn to say sorry before we can tie our shoelaces, yet surprisingly few adults are good at it. The word itself is easy; what is difficult is everything that has to surround it. A useful way to think about an apology is to treat it not so much as a performance of regret as an attempt to repair something that has been damaged. Seen in that light, several familiar habits turn out to work against us. The first is the apology that hinges on the word 'if', as in being sorry if someone happened to feel hurt, which quietly shifts the responsibility onto the person who was wronged. The second is the apology with an explanation attached. Explaining why you were late or why you snapped may feel like honesty, but unless the other person has asked for it, it usually sounds like a defence. The third is apologising too much: a flood of self-criticism that forces the injured party to comfort the person who hurt them. By contrast, apologies that genuinely land tend to share a few features. They name the specific thing that went wrong rather than gesturing vaguely at everything. They acknowledge its effect on the other person without arguing about whether that effect was reasonable. And, where possible, they offer something concrete: to replace what was broken, to change a habit, or simply to do better next time. None of this guarantees forgiveness, nor should it. An apology is an offer, not a transaction, and the other person is entitled to take their time. What a good apology does do is make forgiveness easier to give. Perhaps the most underrated ingredient is timing. Apologising too quickly can sound like an attempt to close the subject, while waiting too long allows resentment to settle in. The best moment is usually once you understand what you did, and before the other person has had to ask.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main point about apologies?
options: An apology is only sincere if it includes a full explanation
A good apology focuses on repairing harm rather than on showing how sorry you feel
People should always apologise as quickly as possible after any mistake
A well-made apology guarantees that the other person will forgive you
questions.evidence: to treat it not so much as a performance of regret as an attempt to repair something that has been damaged

questions.prompt: Why can apologising too much be a problem?
options: It makes the person who was hurt look after the person who hurt them
It takes so long that the other person stops listening
It makes the original mistake seem more serious than it was
It gives the other person a reason to refuse to forgive
questions.evidence: a flood of self-criticism that forces the injured party to comfort the person who hurt them

vocabulary.example: She wrote him a letter full of regret.
It took him years to acknowledge that he had been wrong.
Friendship should never feel like a transaction.
You are entitled to change your mind.
Sleep is the most underrated part of studying well.

expressions.note: 过去分词开头的固定说法，用来引出换个视角后的新结论，书面语常用。

expressions.text: turn out to work against us
expressions.note: turn out to + 动词表示“结果是……”；work against sb 指“对……不利”。
with sth attached 原指“附件”，这里比喻道歉后面“挂着”借口。
段落间引出对照的一方，议论文和说明文都常用。
接在否定句后表示“这样才是对的”，简短有力：It won't fix everything, nor should it.
settle in 原指“安顿下来”，这里形容负面情绪慢慢扎根。

knowledge.quote: unless the other person has asked for it, it usually sounds like a defence
knowledge.explanation: unless 引出唯一的例外：“除非对方问起，否则解释听起来就像辩解”。unless 从句本身用肯定形式，不要再加 not。

knowledge.quote: Explaining why you were late or why you snapped may feel like honesty
knowledge.explanation: 动名词短语 Explaining why ... 作主语，指“解释原因”这一行为；后文的 Apologising too quickly can sound like ... 也是动名词作主语，用来比较不同做法。

knowledge.quote: A useful way to think about an apology is to treat it not so much as a performance of regret as an attempt to repair something that has been damaged.
knowledge.explanation: to think about 修饰 way，to treat 作表语说明“这个方法是什么”，to repair 修饰 attempt。一句里三个不定式各司其职，是 C1 写作中很实用的结构。

speaking: 用 1 分钟说说你收到过的最好或最差的一次道歉，它为什么有效或无效，用上 By contrast 和一个 unless 句。
writing: 写一封 150–200 词的道歉信，向朋友为一次失约道歉：说清具体做错了什么、它带来的影响，并提出一个具体的补救办法，避免用 sorry if。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 ..., but unless ..., it usually ... 说明一个看似好意的行为在什么情况下会适得其反。
task.model: Explaining why you were late or why you snapped may feel like honesty, but unless the other person has asked for it, it usually sounds like a defence.

title: 写日记，值不值得坚持
title_en: Is Keeping a Journal Worth the Effort?
summary_zh: 一篇考试风格的议论文：作者认为写日记值得，但理由不是“保存回忆”，而是“写下来才能想清楚”；并回应了“费时间、越写越钻牛角尖”的反对意见。
body: Keeping a journal is one of those habits that almost everyone admires and hardly anyone sustains. Bookshops are full of handsome notebooks bought with good intentions and abandoned within weeks. The question, then, is whether writing about your own life is genuinely worth the effort. I would argue that it is, though not for the reasons usually given. The most common case for journaling is that it preserves memories. This is true, but it is also the weakest argument, since our phones now do much of that work for us. The stronger case is that writing forces a kind of thinking that rarely happens in our heads. While a worry can circle endlessly in the mind, it has to take a definite shape on the page, and once it has a shape, it can be examined, questioned and sometimes dismissed. In this sense, a journal works more like a workshop than an archive. There are, admittedly, reasonable objections. Critics point out that journaling takes time that most people do not have, and that dwelling on one's feelings can turn reflection into self-absorption. Some people find that writing about a bad day simply makes them live through it twice. These concerns deserve to be taken seriously, but they are arguments about how to keep a journal rather than whether to keep one. A few lines written at the end of the day take minutes, not hours. Focusing on what you might do differently, rather than on how badly things went, keeps the exercise practical instead of self-indulgent. Nor is anyone obliged to write every day; a journal opened only when something needs untangling is still doing its job. In the end, the value of a journal lies not in the quality of the prose or the regularity of the entries, but in the habit of pausing to ask what actually happened and what it meant. That habit is worth cultivating, and for most of us, a pen and a few blank pages remain the simplest way to practise it.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main argument?
options: Journals are valuable mainly because they preserve our memories
Writing things down helps us think more clearly than we can in our heads
Journaling is only worth it if you write every single day
Phones have made traditional journals completely unnecessary
questions.evidence: The stronger case is that writing forces a kind of thinking that rarely happens in our heads.

questions.prompt: How does the writer respond to the critics' objections?
options: By claiming that the critics have never tried keeping a journal
By agreeing that journaling wastes time for busy people
By arguing that the problems can be solved by changing how you write
By insisting that bad days should never be written about
questions.evidence: they are arguments about how to keep a journal rather than whether to keep one

vocabulary.example: Nobody sustains that kind of energy for a whole week.
We found an abandoned bicycle behind the station.
There's no point dwelling on a mistake you can't change.
You're not obliged to answer every message straight away.
Patience is a quality worth cultivating.

expressions.note: with good intentions 常暗示“结果没做到”，带一点自嘲。
is it worth the effort? 是议论文提出问题的常见方式。
take shape 指想法、计划逐渐成形，加 definite 强调“清晰明确”。
议论文让步时的礼貌说法，先肯定对方，再转折反驳。
口语也常用：The old phone is still doing its job.
worth + 动名词，表示“值得……”，比 should be cultivated 更自然。

knowledge.quote: Focusing on what you might do differently, rather than on how badly things went, keeps the exercise practical instead of self-indulgent.
knowledge.explanation: 动名词短语 Focusing on ... 作主语，中间插入 rather than ... 形成对比，谓语 keeps 用单数。用动名词主语提出一种“做法”，是议论文回应反方时的利器。

knowledge.quote: While a worry can circle endlessly in the mind, it has to take a definite shape on the page
knowledge.explanation: while 在这里表示对比（“而”），不是“当……时”：脑子里的担忧可以无限打转，而纸上的必须成形。后面的 once it has a shape 则是时间/条件状语从句。

knowledge.quote: These concerns deserve to be taken seriously, but they are arguments about how to keep a journal rather than whether to keep one.
knowledge.explanation: deserve to be taken 是不定式的被动形式；how to keep / whether to keep 是“疑问词 + 不定式”，把“怎么做”和“要不要做”区分开，是反驳时非常精准的表达。

speaking: 用 1 分钟回答：你觉得写日记（或记手账）值得吗？先表明立场，再说一个反对意见并回应它，用上 deserve to be taken seriously 和 rather than。
writing: 写一篇 250–300 词的议论文，题目“Is it worth learning to cook?”，要有明确论点、让步段和结论，至少用一个动名词主语和一个 while 对比句。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 they are arguments about how to ... rather than whether to ... 回应一个你听过的反对意见。
task.model: they are arguments about how to keep a journal rather than whether to keep one

title: 社区烹饪课体验评测
title_en: Review: Six Thursdays at a Community Cooking Class
summary_zh: 作者在社区中心上了六周晚间烹饪课：老师不给精确配方，要大家边尝边调；厨房小、设备旧，但最后的共餐时光让陌生人成了朋友。读完你能学会写一篇有褒有贬的体验评测。
body: I signed up for the Thursday evening cooking class at our local community centre expecting to pick up a few recipes. Six weeks later, I came away with rather more than that, along with a few complaints worth mentioning. The class is run by Dimitra, a former restaurant cook whose teaching style might best be described as affectionate impatience. She has no interest in recipes measured to the gram. Instead, she wants her students to taste constantly, to adjust as they go and to trust their own judgement, which is unnerving at first for anyone used to following instructions line by line. Each session is built around a single dish, from a simple lentil soup to a surprisingly ambitious fish stew, and the group cooks in pairs before sitting down together to eat whatever has been produced. It is in that final half hour that the class really comes alive. Strangers who arrived barely saying hello end up arguing cheerfully about how much garlic is too much. If the cooking is the official lesson, the shared meal is the hidden one. There are drawbacks, however. Because the kitchen is small, you can spend almost as much time on busy evenings waiting for the oven as actually using it. The equipment, while perfectly adequate, has clearly seen better days, and anyone hoping to learn advanced techniques will be disappointed. Unless you are genuinely a beginner, or at least a nervous cook, the early sessions may feel slow. Yet these are minor criticisms of something that does exactly what it sets out to do. The class makes no attempt to turn anyone into a chef. Its aim is to make cooking feel less like a test and more like a conversation, and on that measure it succeeds. I left with three dishes I now make without looking anything up and, more unexpectedly, a standing arrangement to make dinner with my cooking partner from the second week. It is warmly recommended, especially for anyone who cooks alone more often than they would like.

questions.prompt: What does the reviewer seem to value most about the class?
options: The chance to learn advanced restaurant techniques
The modern, well-equipped kitchen
The way it builds confidence and brings strangers together
The precise recipes that students can take home
questions.evidence: Its aim is to make cooking feel less like a test and more like a conversation, and on that measure it succeeds.

questions.prompt: What does "has clearly seen better days" suggest about the equipment?
options: It is brand new but difficult to use
It is old and worn, although it still does the job
It is too advanced for most beginners
It breaks down so often that it is unusable
questions.evidence: The equipment, while perfectly adequate, has clearly seen better days

vocabulary.example: She gave her old dog an affectionate pat on the head.

vocabulary.meaning: 令人不安的；让人心里发慌的
vocabulary.example: The silence in the empty house was a little unnerving.
I trust her judgement when it comes to choosing restaurants.
Living in the city centre has a few drawbacks, such as the noise.
The hotel room was small but adequate for one night.

expressions.note: worth + 动名词；评测里常用来引出优点或缺点：One more thing worth mentioning is ...
as you go 表示“在进行的过程中”，做饭、学习、做项目都能用。

expressions.meaning: 一行一行地；逐字逐句地
expressions.note: 形容严格按照说明做事，常带一点“死板”的意味。

expressions.meaning: 变得生动起来；活跃起来
expressions.note: 形容场面、城市、故事突然有了生气：The street comes alive at night.
委婉地说某物老旧破损，带点幽默，评测和日常聊天都常用。
does what it sets out to do 是评测里夸“名副其实、达到目标”的常用说法。

knowledge.quote: she wants her students to taste constantly, to adjust as they go and to trust their own judgement
knowledge.explanation: want sb to do sth：三个并列的不定式说明老师希望学生做什么；并列时每个 to 都可以保留，读起来节奏更清楚。

knowledge.quote: Because the kitchen is small, you can spend almost as much time on busy evenings waiting for the oven as actually using it.
knowledge.explanation: because 引导原因状语从句放在句首，先说原因再说后果；主句里 as much time ... waiting ... as using 是同级比较，突出等待时间之长。

knowledge.quote: Unless you are genuinely a beginner, or at least a nervous cook, the early sessions may feel slow.
knowledge.explanation: unless = if you are not：“除非你真是新手，否则前几节课可能会觉得慢”。评测中用 unless 精准划出“适合人群”，比 if you are not 更简洁。

speaking: 用 1 分钟评价你上过的一门课或参加过的一次活动，先说优点，再说一个缺点，最后说适合谁，用上 seen better days 或 does what it sets out to do。
writing: 写一篇 200–250 词的体验评测（课程、餐厅、健身房等），要有优点、缺点和推荐对象，至少用一次 Unless you are ... 和一次 Because ...。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 If A is the official ..., B is the hidden one 写出一件事“表面的目的”和“真正的收获”。
task.model: If the cooking is the official lesson, the shared meal is the hidden one.
